article_title: The battle for Charlie Kirk’s legacy
summary: The episode examines whether young voters will stay Republican after activist Charlie Kirk’s death and if the fight over his legacy could cost Donald Trump votes in the 2024 midterms. Hearings begin to decide if prosecutors have enough evidence to charge alleged killer Tyler Robinson. The show notes far‑right conspiracy theories, Kirk’s past endorsements, and the GOP’s challenge retaining the youth vote amid a waning administration.

article_title: Renewables company ZEN Energy enters voluntary administration
summary: South Australian renewable‑energy firm ZEN Energy, which held a decade‑long power contract with the state government and was involved in solar farms and battery projects, has entered voluntary administration after wholesale electricity volatility undermined its viability. Administrator McGrathNicol is assessing the business. The SA government says electricity supply to its facilities continues via AGL and a new supplier will be procured. ZEN previously withdrew from a Queensland renewable precinct.

article_title: AI and Iran will speed up the energy transition
summary: Iran forced two ships to turn back, asserting control of the Strait of Hormuz, raising shipping costs and prompting greater reliance on renewables. Meanwhile Chinese firm Z.ai released the open‑weight AI model GLM‑5.2, matching ChatGPT at a fraction of the price, spurring wider AI use and higher electricity demand. Together, tighter oil transport and cheap AI are expected to accelerate the global energy transition.

article_title: Putin Faces Crisis as Fuel Shortages Ripple Through Russia...
summary: Ukrainian drone strikes have hit more than 50 Russian oil refineries, depots and terminals since March, cutting June crude processing by 25% and gasoline output by 17%. About one‑third of refining capacity is offline, prompting fuel rationing, long queues and portable toilets at stations across the country, even in untouched Siberia. Putin acknowledged the shortages as “temporary.” Repairs will take months, so shortages are expected to persist through the summer.

article_title: In Pamplona With The Bulls As Hemingway’s “The Sun Also Rises” Turns 100
summary: The 2024 San Fermin festival marks the 100th anniversary of Ernest Hemingway’s 1926 novel *The Sun Also Rises*, which made Pamplona’s bull runs famous worldwide. The celebration began with fireworks and will feature eight runs. Americans remain the largest foreign group of participants (16% in 2022). Chicago writer‑runner Bill Hillmann, gored three times, now teaches the book. Hemingway’s legacy is praised for popularizing the event but also criticized for glorifying bullfighting and spurring overtourism.

article_title: Saudis must recognise Israel for nuclear deal, says Trump
summary: President Trump said the US‑Saudi civil nuclear agreement will only be approved if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords and recognises Israel. The White House confirmed the condition, noting the deal involves peaceful nuclear cooperation and safeguards and will go to Congress for review, with IAEA verification. Saudi officials have not responded, while experts warn of proliferation risks; Israel welcomed the prospect of Saudi recognition.

article_title: Ready to 'conquer Earth' - Joshua embraces comeback spotlight
summary: Anthony Joshua (36) will return to the ring in Jeddah on Saturday, facing Albanian‑born heavyweight Kristian Prenga in his first fight since the December car crash in Nigeria that killed two close friends. A win would move Joshua toward a potential all‑British showdown with Tyson Fury, provided Fury also wins his bout in Thailand. Joshua appeared relaxed at the press conference, thanked fans and said he’s “ready to conquer Earth.”

article_title: Why hasn't the global economy completely collapsed?
summary: The global economy avoided collapse after the U.S. attack on Iran, with oil prices slipping to about $70 a barrel but staying above pre‑crisis levels. A 3.7 million‑barrel‑per‑day surplus and 8.2 billion barrels of storage, plus China cutting imports 40 %, eased pressure. Countries diversified supply—U.S., Venezuela, Brazil, Singapore, and Gulf reroutes—while lower energy intensity and renewables helped absorb the shock. Poorer nations lack such buffers, prompting concerns about future energy security.

summary: Somalia’s communications minister, Ahmed Osman Dirie, warned that WhatsApp’s upcoming username feature could hinder the country’s fight against al‑Shabab and increase financial fraud, as it would make users harder to trace than phone‑number‑linked accounts. He has asked Meta for guarantees that the change won’t erode digital traceability. WhatsApp says the feature isn’t live yet, will still require a phone number and includes anti‑scam safeguards, echoing similar concerns raised by India.

summary: Yemen’s Iran‑backed Houthi fighters have attacked and warned off ships in the Red Sea, forcing vessels to avoid the Bab el‑Mandeb strait and threatening a key Europe‑Asia trade route. The attacks come amid 13 nights of U.S. airstrikes on Iranian targets, ongoing U.S.–Iran conflict, and a new U.S.‑backed Saudi civilian nuclear programme that raises regional arms‑race fears, heightening economic and security risks across the Middle East.

summary: Federal officials have linked shredded iceberg lettuce from Mexico, served at Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia, to a multistate Cyclospora outbreak. The CDC warned consumers not to eat the lettuce, and the FDA traced it to a single supplier, Taylor Fresh Foods (Taylor Farms). Taco Bell halted use of the product, and the supplier is removing the lettuce from the U.S. market. The outbreak has produced over 5,000 cases in Michigan, more than 2,000 elsewhere, over 100 hospitalizations and no deaths.

Hikers lost near Kosciuszko found by artificial intelligence drone
summary: Two hikers lost in Kosciuszko National Park were rescued by Fire and Rescue NSW using an AI-powered drone. This marked the first successful use of the drone's AI detection system by FRNSW to locate a missing hiker. The drone used thermal imaging to find the men 500 metres off track and communicate with them, significantly reducing search time and rescuer risk. FRNSW plans to improve the technology for future emergencies.

article_title: Hikers lost near Kosciuszko found by artificial intelligence drone
summary: Two hikers in their early 20s went missing at 7 p.m. on Tuesday while on the Dead Horse Gap track, 35 km southwest of Jindabyne in Kosciuszko National Park. Fire and Rescue NSW deployed an AI‑driven remote‑piloted drone with thermal imaging, which located the men about 500 m off the trail. Using the drone’s speaker, rescuers guided them out within five hours; they suffered mild exposure and declined treatment. This was the first successful FRNSW rescue using the drone’s AI detection system.

The move follows former TV host Jennifer Baing’s experience of AI‑fabricated lingerie photos used in fake giveaways, which she says threaten her reputation and safety. Police, with only seven cyber officers, report a surge in AI‑related scams, while Pacific neighbours are also tightening cybercrime laws and urging community awareness and victim support.

Trump claims the pledge will lower household bills, though analysts warn electricity demand could push rates up 15‑40% by 2030. Bipartisan opposition has spurred state bans and a House Energy Committee bill to make data centers cover grid‑upgrade costs.

summary: Chinese AI start-up Moonshot has unveiled Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter model, claiming it rivals top American firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. Set for open-source release on July 27, Kimi K3 is touted as the world's first open-source model in its class, capable of coding, knowledge work, and reasoning. Third-party evaluations show it performing on par with leading US models, suggesting China is rapidly narrowing the AI capabilities gap.

article_title: Will AI help you do your job or replace you?
summary: AI firms claim their tools can replace human labor, prompting major companies to invest in “AI agents” that could cut headcount. Economists warn of large‑scale displacement, and recent data shows LLMs now handle complex software coding, contract analysis and other tasks previously done by humans. A U.S. study finds employment for 22‑25‑year‑olds fell 2.7% overall and up to 12.8% in AI‑exposed sectors such as finance, software and creative work. The UK’s service‑heavy economy appears similarly vulnerable. Token usage has surged, driving high costs that are forcing firms to ration AI and turn to cheaper Chinese models.

article_title: ICE arrests Australian accused of illegally voting in US elections
summary: Denise Nataly Migliore, a 51‑year‑old Australian living in Franklinton, Louisiana, was arrested at a New Orleans federal courthouse and indicted on four counts for illegally voting in the 2022 and 2024 U.S. federal elections and for making false statements to register. ICE and federal partners led the investigation. If convicted, she faces up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a $250,000 fine. The Australian government is providing consular assistance.

article_title: Why hasn't the global economy completely collapsed?
summary: The global economy has surprisingly avoided collapse despite ongoing conflict and a 20% cut in oil supply due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. This resilience is attributed to several factors, including China significantly reducing its oil purchases by 40% due to existing large stockpiles and a global oil surplus before the crisis. Additionally, countries rapidly diversified their oil suppliers and transport routes, with increased exports from the US, Venezuela, and Brazil, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE utilizing alternative pipelines. The world economy has also become less reliant on oil due to a shift towards less energy-intensive services, improved energy efficiency, and the growth of renewable energy sources. While a global recession was avoided, the crisis has contributed to higher inflation and slower growth, particularly impacting poorer countries with fewer energy reserves.

article_title: Report finds Brisbane has country's best nightlife — if it's Thursday
summary: A report commissioned by Australia's capital city mayors has ranked Brisbane as having the best nightlife in Australia, specifically on Thursdays. This shift is attributed to changing work habits post-pandemic, with Thursday becoming the busiest day for office workers. Brisbane's drinking economy has seen a 14% surge in venues, contrasting with a national decline. Additionally, Thursday is Brisbane's late-night shopping day, with 41% of retailers open in the evening. The report also highlights initiatives like fairy lights and security cameras contributing to the city's vibrant night-time economy.

article_title: SUPREME LEADER WARNING
summary: The U.S. military launched new airstrikes against Iran on Sunday, stating the action was to "swiftly punish" Iran's Revolutionary Guard after an attack in Jordan killed two American service members. These strikes aimed to degrade Iran's ability to restrict oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran had effectively closed after the war began on February 28. Iran's state media reported strikes in southern Iran, near the Strait of Hormuz, and in Khuzestan province. Separately, a base of an Iranian Kurdish dissident group in Iraq was struck by a drone, wounding eight members. Iran's supreme leader warned of "unforgettable lessons" if the U.S. continued attacks, and an Iranian negotiator stated Tehran was suspending commitments to an interim deal.

article_title: Iran's demands over the Strait of Hormuz would set a dangerous precedent, Rubio warns Asian leaders
summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Asian leaders that Iran's demand to control and collect tolls in the Strait of Hormuz would threaten the global economy and set a dangerous precedent. Speaking at an ASEAN meeting in Manila, Rubio also renewed allegations that Iran has reneged on commitments under a collapsed interim ceasefire deal. Russia and Australia expressed concern over the Middle East conflict's impact on the global economy and energy markets. Additionally, Rubio met with Quad partners to discuss countering China's influence and addressed recent altercations between Chinese and Filipino forces with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. Rubio is also scheduled to meet with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to discuss the war in Ukraine.

article_title: Why WhatsApp usernames could upset Somalia's anti-terror fight
summary: Somalia's government has expressed concern to the BBC about WhatsApp's upcoming feature allowing users to chat via usernames instead of phone numbers, citing potential security risks. Communications and Technology Minister Ahmed Osman Dirie stated that this could hinder efforts to trace criminals and counter Islamist militants like al-Shabab, who use WhatsApp for operations. Dirie also highlighted the risk of financial fraud and scams in Somalia's mobile money-reliant economy due to untraceable usernames. WhatsApp responded that the feature is not yet live, users will still need a phone number for the app, and built-in safeguards against scams are included. Somalia, like India, is seeking further assurances and specific safeguards from Meta to ensure the feature does not erode digital traceability or increase financial fraud.

article_title: Houthi attacks raise fears of wider Middle East conflict and more global economic damage
summary: Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping are escalating fears of a wider Middle East conflict and global economic damage. These attacks, which have targeted Saudi vessels and disrupted traffic through the Bab El Mandeb Strait, threaten a crucial maritime route from Europe to Asia. This comes amidst ongoing US-Iran strikes and concerns about a potential regional arms race following a deal for Saudi Arabia's nuclear industry. The combined disruptions to key shipping lanes like the Strait of Hormuz and Bab El Mandeb are expected to significantly impact global supply chains and prices.

article_title: Expanding Sydney's tree canopy could save $1b a year in health costs
summary: A new report by the Committee for Sydney suggests that increasing Sydney's tree canopy could save $1 billion in annual health costs. The report proposes creating "greenways" using publicly owned land to plant new trees and create public spaces, particularly in areas slated for increased housing density. This initiative aims to combat urban heat island effects and address the uneven distribution of tree canopy across the city, which currently stands at 21.7%, well below the NSW government's 40% target by 2036. The NSW government has formed a new committee to streamline green infrastructure projects and has already begun transferring land for protected open space, aligning with the report's recommendations.

article_title: Concerns for lost health services under sale to Calvary
summary: Doctors are concerned about a potential loss of services if Hobart Private Hospital is sold to Catholic healthcare provider Calvary, which would create a monopoly in Tasmania's major centers. They warn that Calvary's policies would prohibit abortions, gender-affirming care, and certain contraceptive procedures currently offered at Hobart Private. Tasmania's Health Minister is working to ensure these services remain available, exploring options within the public system or with other private providers. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) is expected to decide on the sale by July 28, considering both the potential service loss and the lack of other buyers. Healthcare providers are wary of the public system's ability to absorb these services, given existing pressures and budget cuts.

article_title: RUNS FOR THE BORDER: Lettuce at TACO BELL in 5 states confirmed as a source of diarrhea parasite...
summary: Federal health officials have confirmed that lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in five states is the source of a cyclospora outbreak. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advised consumers not to eat shredded iceberg lettuce from Taco Bell in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia. Taylor Fresh Foods, identified as a supplier, is voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market. Taco Bell has committed to using a different lettuce supplier. The investigation is ongoing, and other businesses may also be linked to the outbreak.

article_title: ICE officer in Maine shooting has history of violent behavior...
summary: An ICE officer, David Brouillette, fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. Relatives claim Brouillette has a history of violent behavior and serious mental health issues, including diagnoses of severe bipolar disorder and attention deficit disorder as a child. They accuse him of attacking women and making violent threats, with one ex-wife sharing a voicemail where he suggested she should have her throat slit. Brouillette's ex-wife and daughter stated he admitted to the shooting, claiming self-defense. ICE has not released the officer's name but stated he has nearly a decade of federal law enforcement experience and required training.

article_title: How we know this Mitch McConnell photo isn't AI-generated
summary: A photo shared by US Senator Mitch McConnell, showing him recovering after a fall, has sparked speculation about its authenticity, with some claiming it is AI-generated. However, there is no evidence to support these claims. The 84-year-old Republican had been hospitalized after a fall and mild pneumonia, leading to questions about his health after a period out of the public eye. BBC Verify's Jake Horton has explained how the photo can be determined as genuine.

article_title: Legionnaires' outbreak hits New York as officials rush to test water towers
summary: An outbreak of Legionnaires' disease in New York City's Upper East Side has sickened 46 people, with 22 hospitalized. The city has linked the infections, a serious type of pneumonia, to contaminated water cooling towers. Officials have tested all cooling towers in the affected area, finding Legionella bacteria in 31, and have disinfected 19. Residents express concern, with some taking precautions like wearing masks and keeping windows closed. The city has implemented an "aggressive" plan to address the outbreak, requiring immediate disinfection of towers upon a positive test result.
